claims.text: Adding approximately 1–2 at.% yttrium to a phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy will improve its glass-forming ability.
Adding approximately 1–2 at.% yttrium will enhance the thermal stability of the alloy's amorphous state.
The proposed baseline alloy has marginal glass-forming ability and crystallizes rapidly upon heating.
Yttrium should be introduced at 1–2 at.% during alloy melting and distributed homogeneously before rapid solidification.
Modified and baseline samples should be prepared under inert atmosphere using otherwise similar melt-quench and cooling conditions.
Thermal stability should be assessed by DSC at approximately 20 K/min and by sub-Tg annealing.
Yttrium addition will form localized Y–P chemical-bonding clusters.
Yttrium may also form localized bonding clusters with other alloying elements.
The localized clusters will enhance atomic packing and disrupt long-range order.
The localized clusters will impede the formation or activity of crystallization nuclei.
Yttrium has a large atomic size relative to the relevant alloy constituents.
Yttrium has a strong bonding preference for phosphorus.
Yttrium addition increases atomic-size mismatch and chemical heterogeneity.
The increased size mismatch and chemical heterogeneity stabilize dense random atomic arrangements and raise the energy barrier for crystallization.
The yttrium-modified alloy will have a lower critical cooling rate for glass formation than the yttrium-free baseline.
The yttrium-modified alloy will have a higher crystallization-onset temperature than the yttrium-free baseline.
The beneficial effect is expected only within a narrow yttrium-content window of approximately 1–2 at.%.
Higher yttrium concentrations may precipitate Y-rich crystalline phases and thereby reduce amorphous stability.
The magnitude of the effect may depend on the alloy's overall composition and processing conditions.

Failure to obtain a statistically significant improvement in glass-forming ability or crystallization-onset temperature, together with no structural evidence of improved amorphous stability, would falsify the hypothesis.
